noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to describe the different structures formed by giant lattices of carbon atoms, including graphite, diamond and graphene, and discuss the applications of each

primer.text: Carbon's allotropes prove that arrangement beats ingredient: the same atoms build scratch-proof diamond, shear-easy graphite and one-atom-thin graphene. Giant covalent lattices melt ferociously high; only graphite conducts, banking one spare electron per atom; graphene inherits the sheet's talents without the stack. This note compares all three structures, bond by bond.

lessons.title: One element, many personalities
sourceHeadings: Covalent bonding & giant covalent lattice structures
lessons.opening: Allotropes are pure substances built from one element whose atoms connect in different arrangements - and carbon is the master of the game. Every carbon allotrope is a giant covalent lattice melting ferociously high, yet graphite shears soft while diamond scratches everything, and only graphite conducts, because only graphite leaves electrons spare.
keyPoints: Allotropes contain only one element but differ in bonding arrangement and so in physical properties.
Melting or boiling a giant covalent lattice takes very high temperatures: countless strong covalent bonds link the whole structure.
Diamond and silicon(IV) oxide are hard: breaking their 3D networks is difficult.
Graphite is soft because the forces between its carbon layers are weak.
Graphite conducts via delocalised electrons between layers; diamond's four bonded electrons leave none free.

low.restatement: Same atoms, different wiring: how the carbons connect decides whether the material melts high, scratches glass or writes on paper.
low.analogy: The same bricks build a fused dome (diamond) or stacked slabs (graphite) - construction, not ingredient, sets the behaviour.
low.examPointer: Allotrope questions are structure questions: name the bonding arrangement first, the property second.

medium.restatement: Property differences trace to connectivity and the weakest link: networks of strong covalent bonds melt high, hardness reads the 3D continuity of those bonds, and conductivity appears only where the bonding leaves electrons unassigned.
medium.analogy: One road network, three traffic rules: fully connected grids jam nothing (hard), stacked roads slide at the joins (soft), and only networks with spare lanes let current flow.
medium.examPointer: Pair every property with its structural cause - the examiner marks the cause, not the property alone.

check.stem: What defines two substances as allotropes of each other?

options.text: They contain the same element bonded in different arrangements
options.explanation: Carbon's diamond and graphite are the classic pair.

options.text: They contain the same atoms in the same arrangement
options.explanation: Identical arrangements would be the same substance.

options.text: They contain different elements with similar properties
options.explanation: Allotropes are single-element substances.
The difference is structural and physical, not cosmetic.

check.stem: Why do giant covalent lattices melt at very high temperatures?

options.text: A large number of strong covalent bonds must be broken throughout the structure
options.explanation: Melting means dismantling bonds across the whole network.

options.text: Weak intermolecular forces hold them together
options.explanation: Weak forces characterise simple molecules, not giant lattices.
Mass is not the mechanism; bonding is.
No ions roam these neutral networks.

check.stem: Which property distinguishes graphite from diamond in terms of electrical behaviour?

options.explanation: Graphite's spare electron roams the layers; diamond's electrons are all bonded.
The conductive member is graphite.
Their electron availability differs.
Graphite's delocalised electrons carry current.

check.stem: Diamond and silicon(IV) oxide are both hard because

options.text: their 3D covalent networks are extremely hard to snap
options.explanation: Hardness reads the strength and continuity of the network.

options.text: their atoms slide easily over each other
options.explanation: Easy sliding makes graphite soft, the opposite case.
They melt very high.

options.text: they contain free electrons that stiffen them
options.explanation: Neither has free electrons; stiffness comes from bonded networks.

check.stem: Graphite is soft because

options.text: the forces between its carbon layers are weak and easily overcome
options.explanation: Layers shear off despite strong in-layer bonding.

options.text: its covalent bonds are individually weak
options.explanation: In-layer covalent bonds are very strong.

options.text: it contains no covalent bonds at all
options.explanation: Every carbon bonds covalently to three neighbours.

options.text: its atoms are arranged in 3D tetrahedra
options.explanation: That describes diamond.

check.stem: Define allotropes.
check.modelAnswer: Allotropes are substances containing only one element whose atoms bond in different arrangements, giving completely different physical properties.

check.stem: State why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
check.modelAnswer: Graphite has delocalised electrons between its carbon layers that move along the layers under a voltage; diamond's four outer electrons per atom are all locked in covalent bonds, leaving none free.

check.stem: Explain why the same element can produce both the hardest and one of the softest natural substances.
check.modelAnswer: Property follows arrangement, not ingredient: diamond ties every atom into a rigid 3D covalent network, while graphite ties atoms only within sheets and lets the sheets rest on weak interlayer forces, so one scratches and the other shears.

check.stem: A lab drawer holds two black pencils 'lead' samples, one conducting and one insulating when tested along the same axis. Assign each to its allotrope and justify.
check.modelAnswer: The conducting sample is graphite - its delocalised electrons run along the layers - and the insulating one is diamond dust, whose electrons are all committed to four covalent bonds with no spare carrier.

lessons.title: Graphite against diamond
lessons.opening: The two heavyweight allotropes part ways at the bonding ledger. Graphite's carbons bond to three neighbours in sheets of hexagons, leaving one free electron per atom that carries current along the layers; strong in-layer bonds meet weak van der Waals forces between layers, so the sheets slide - soft, slippery, conductive. Diamond bonds every carbon to four neighbours in a tetrahedral web of identical, very strong bonds: no spare electrons, no intermolecular forces, extreme hardness.
keyPoints: Graphite bonds each carbon to three others, forming layers of hexagons with one free electron per atom.
The free electrons migrate along the layers and carry charge, so graphite conducts.
Strong covalent bonds run within the layers, but weak van der Waals forces hold layers together, letting them slide.
Diamond bonds each carbon to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement.
Diamond's bonds are all identical and very strong, with no intermolecular forces and no free electrons.

low.restatement: Graphite is three bonds plus one spare electron per atom, stacked in slick sheets; diamond is four bonds per atom, welded into one rigid web.
low.analogy: Stacks of cling film versus a welded jungle gym: the film slides and wraps, the gym neither bends nor lets anything through.
low.examPointer: Quote the bond counts - three and four - and the consequence of each in the same sentence.

medium.restatement: The allotropes diverge at the fourth electron: graphite spends three electrons on in-layer bonds and banks the fourth as a delocalised carrier between the sheets, while diamond commits all four into the tetrahedral network - conductivity, softness and hardness all follow from that single bookkeeping difference.
medium.analogy: Two pay packets: one worker keeps a third of each cheque liquid (graphite's spare electron), the other reinvests everything into a fixed structure (diamond's fourth bond).
medium.examPointer: Name the interlayer force explicitly as van der Waals' forces - 'weak forces' alone is only half the answer.

check.stem: How many other carbon atoms does each carbon touch in graphite?

options.explanation: The fourth outer electron stays free.
That is diamond's arrangement.
Graphite forms hexagonal sheets.
Each atom touches three neighbours, not six.

check.stem: What gives graphite its electrical conductivity?

options.text: Free electrons that migrate along the layers carrying charge
options.explanation: One spare electron per atom moves under a voltage.
No ions exist in graphite.
Weak forces enable sliding, not conduction.
Geometry without free electrons conducts nothing.

check.stem: Why do graphite's layers slide over each other so easily?

options.text: Weak van der Waals' forces between layers are easily overcome
options.explanation: The strong in-layer bonds stay intact while sheets shear.

options.text: The covalent bonds within layers are weak
options.explanation: They are very strong.
Conduction and lubrication are separate effects.
Attraction, weak but real, holds them.

check.stem: In diamond, how many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form?

options.explanation: All four outer electrons are committed.
That is graphite's ledger.
Two bonds would strand the octet.
Eight neighbours exceeds carbon's bonding capacity.

check.stem: Which statement about diamond's bonds is correct?

options.text: All the covalent bonds are identical and very strong, with no intermolecular forces present
options.explanation: A uniform 3D network with nothing weaker inside.

options.text: Alternate bonds are strong and weak
options.explanation: Diamond's bonds are all identical.
No intermolecular forces exist in the network.

options.text: Its bonds break easily under pressure
options.explanation: Diamond is the hardness benchmark.

check.stem: State the bonding arrangement of graphite, including bond count and structure shape.
check.modelAnswer: Each carbon atom bonds to three others, forming layers of hexagons, with one free electron per atom left over.

check.stem: State the bonding arrangement of diamond and its consequence for electrical conduction.
check.modelAnswer: Each carbon bonds to four others in a tetrahedron; with every outer electron in a covalent bond, there are no freely moving electrons and diamond does not conduct.

check.stem: Explain why graphite's in-layer strength and interlayer weakness coexist.
check.modelAnswer: Within a sheet, each carbon invests three strong covalent bonds in its neighbours, but between sheets only weak van der Waals' attractions operate, so the same crystal is brutal to stretch and effortless to shear.

check.stem: Predict which allotrope suits both an electrical contact and a dry lubricant, and explain the shared structural reason.
check.modelAnswer: Graphite serves both: the same delocalised electrons that carry current along layers belong to a structure whose weakly held layers slide under shear - one arrangement, two applications.

lessons.title: Graphene: the single sheet
lessons.opening: Graphene is graphite reduced to its minimum: one isolated layer, a continuous sheet of hexagonally bonded carbon just one atom thick. That makes it effectively a two-dimensional molecule, and its unusual behaviour - the same in-plane conduction as graphite with none of the layer weaknesses - has made it the material of choice for composite materials and electronics research.
keyPoints: Graphene is a single layer of graphite - one continuous hexagonal sheet of carbon atoms.
Its atoms are covalently bonded into one uninterrupted hexagonal layer.
Being one atom thick makes graphene essentially a 2D molecule.
Its very unusual properties suit composite materials and electronics.
It shares graphite's in-plane conduction without any stacked layers to slide.

low.restatement: Take graphite, peel off one sheet, and you have graphene: one atom-thin hexagon mesh with big electronic talents.
low.analogy: One page lifted from a ream: everything that made the ream slippery between pages is gone, leaving the page's own strengths.
low.examPointer: Anchor the definition: 'single layer of graphite' - every fuller answer hangs from that phrase.

medium.restatement: Graphene keeps graphite's per-atom ledger - three covalent bonds and one delocalised electron - but removes the interlayer van der Waals chapter entirely, so conduction and mechanical strength arrive in a strictly two-dimensional membrane.
medium.analogy: The same sheet music (bonding pattern) played by a soloist instead of a stacked choir: the harmony is identical, the physics newly pure.
medium.examPointer: Applications questions want the pair: composite materials and electronics - name both.

check.stem: What exactly is graphene?

options.text: A single layer of graphite - one continuous hexagonal carbon sheet
options.explanation: The definition of record for the material.

options.text: A stack of many graphite layers
options.explanation: Stacks are graphite itself.

options.text: A spherical network of carbon atoms
options.explanation: That describes fullerenes.
That describes diamond.

check.stem: Why is graphene described as a 2D molecule?

options.text: It is only one atom thick
options.explanation: Thickness vanishes at the atomic limit.
Conduction is a consequence, not the definition.
Flatness of the ring is incidental; the sheet's thickness is the point.
Its atoms are covalently bonded throughout.

check.stem: Which applications does the note assign to graphene?

options.explanation: Its unusual properties serve both fields.
Those are bulk graphite applications.
That is diamond's niche.
Neither appears in the graphene material story.

check.stem: How does graphene's bonding compare with graphite's?

options.text: Identical per-atom bonding - three covalent bonds in a hexagonal sheet - just without the stacked layers
options.explanation: Graphene is one graphite layer isolated.

options.text: Four bonds per atom like diamond
options.explanation: Graphene keeps graphite's three-bond ledger.
Both are pure carbon.
In-plane covalent bonds remain strong.

check.stem: A researcher peels successive layers from graphite until reaching one layer. Which property difference should they expect?

options.text: The final single sheet still conducts along its plane but no longer benefits from layer sliding
options.explanation: In-plane electronics remain; the interlayer feature vanishes with the stack.

options.text: The sheet loses its conduction entirely
options.explanation: Graphene retains in-plane conduction.

options.text: The sheet becomes harder than diamond
options.explanation: No such claim holds.
The dimensional change is the whole point.

check.stem: State the structural definition of graphene.
check.modelAnswer: Graphene is a single layer of graphite: a sheet of carbon atoms covalently bonded into one continuous hexagonal layer.

check.stem: State the two application areas named for graphene.
Explain why graphene's single-sheet structure gives it unusual properties compared with bulk graphite.
check.modelAnswer: All of graphite's interlayer behaviour - sliding, weak van der Waals failure planes - disappears at one atom thick, leaving a pure 2D covalent membrane whose electron behaviour and strength are unlike any bulk material.

check.stem: A composite engineer wants a conductive, one-atom-thin additive for a polymer film. Choose the allotrope and give the two structural facts that justify it.
check.modelAnswer: Graphene: it is one continuous hexagonal carbon sheet (so one atom thin) and its per-atom free electron conduction runs along the sheet, exactly what a conductive additive needs.

glossary.definition: One of the structurally different forms of the same element, such as graphite and diamond for carbon.
A structure where huge numbers of atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds throughout.
A single one-atom-thick hexagonal sheet of covalently bonded carbon atoms.
